lesson.title: The TCP IP Model: The Leaner Stack That Actually Runs the Internet
lesson.summary: The TCP IP model is the practical, four layer architecture that the real Internet was built on, simpler than OSI and organized directly around the protocols engineers actually deploy.
lesson.body:
While the OSI model was still being standardized on paper, engineers working on the ARPANET and its successors were already building a working internetwork, and they organized it around a simpler set of layers directly tied to the protocols they were actually writing. That architecture is known as the TCP IP model, named after its two most central protocols, Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol. It is described in early Internet standards documents, including RFC 1122, as having four layers: Link, Internet, Transport, and Application.

The Link layer covers everything involved in moving data across one specific physical connection or local network, roughly combining what OSI splits into its Physical and Data Link layers. The Internet layer, implemented primarily by IP, handles addressing and routing across multiple interconnected networks, corresponding closely to OSI's Network layer. The Transport layer, implemented primarily by TCP and its counterpart UDP, handles delivery between specific programs, corresponding closely to OSI's Transport layer. The Application layer covers everything from web browsing to email to file transfer, folding together what OSI treats as three separate layers: Session, Presentation, and Application.

This four layer approach was not a simplification for its own sake, it reflects how the protocols were actually engineered. Real Internet protocols rarely respected clean boundaries between session management, presentation formatting, and application logic, so TCP IP simply did not force a separation the working protocols did not naturally have. Because the two models grew from different goals, one a formal international standard, the other a working engineering project, some networking courses and textbooks teach a five layer version of TCP IP instead, splitting Link into separate Physical and Data Link layers so it lines up one to one with OSI's bottom two layers. Both four layer and five layer descriptions are common, and both are describing the same actual Internet architecture.

A worked example shows the practical difference from OSI. When a browser fetches a web page, in TCP IP terms that is simply: an Application layer protocol, HTTP, handed to the Transport layer, TCP, handed to the Internet layer, IP, handed to the Link layer, typically Ethernet or Wi-Fi. There is no separate Session or Presentation layer protocol most engineers ever have to name, those concerns, when they exist at all, are just handled within the application itself.

Both OSI and TCP IP are, at their core, expressions of the same underlying idea covered earlier: layered architecture, with each layer relying on protocols to talk to its counterpart and encapsulation to hand data down the stack. OSI offers a more granular, standardized reference vocabulary. TCP IP offers a leaner model matching what was actually built and is still running the Internet today. With both models established, the next three chapters look closely at three of the layers they share: physical, data link, and network.
